newsitem.title: UK: Pensions shock could hit Britain in EMU - MPs.
newsitem.headline: Pensions shock could hit Britain in EMU - MPs.

text.p: A parliamentary committee warned on Thursday that huge unfunded pension liabilities in other European Union states could harm Britain if it joined a single currency by either raising interest rates or fuelling inflation.

The all-party Social Security Committee called on the government to press Brussels to take the liabilities into account when deciding which EU countries are eligible for Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

Britain is unusual in the European Union (EU) in that most pensioners derive most of their income from occupational pension schemes, usually run by employers who fund them through a mixture of company and employee contributions.
In a report, the committee said "The extent of unfunded pension liabilities in certain of our European partner countries casts serious doubt upon the long-term sustainability of their finances."

It noted that a recent Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) report had assessed the net present value of public pension schemes in Britain at around 19 percent of gross domestic product.
By contrast, the figures for France, Italy and Germany were around 98, 113 and 139 percent, respectively.
The report noted there had already been popular unrest in France and Germany at government attempts to curtail social security provisions.

"It is likely, therefore, that alternative ways of meeting current costs will be employed. One risk would be that the European Central Bank would come under pressure to relax monetary policy by printing money," it said.
"Another risk is that countries might seek to borrow their way out of financial pressures caused by rising social security bills," the report added.
If this happened and Britain had joined Monetary Union,it said "bond issuance from hard-pressed European Union governments would raise (other things being equal) yields on Euro-denominated bonds."
This would increase British industrial costs and interest rates and damage employment prospects.

"In this way, taxpayers in the United Kingdom, whose pensions derive largely from funded occupational pension schemes, could find themselves subsidising the large unfunded pension liabilities of other member states -- even with no element of Fiscal Union in the EU," the committee said.
It recommended that Britain press EU Finance Ministers to commission experts to produce figures on unfunded pension liabilities in member states.
It said these data should then be taken into account "in the decision to be made in 1998 on which countries will be eligible for Economic and Monetary Union". -- London Newsroom +44 171 5427767
